title: apexe tool overlay
description: A curated, reviewed description of one variant of one CLI command. Overlays exist because heuristic scanning cannot be authoritative for system built-ins: their --help is often a single bundled usage line, their man pages are prose, and neither states mutual exclusion or value types. An overlay is keyed by (command, variant, version_range).

allOf.description: A "verified" claim must carry the record of how it was checked. Without provenance, a verified + authoritative overlay replaces the whole scan result with an assertion nobody can re-check.
vendor-docs provenance has no re-runnable command, so it must cite what was read instead.

schema_version.description: Overlay format version. Only "1.0" is currently accepted.

command.description: Command name this overlay describes, e.g. "ls" (never a path).

variant.description: Which implementation of the command this overlay describes. A command name does not identify a program: /bin/ls on macOS is BSD, /usr/bin/ls on GNU/Linux is coreutils, and Homebrew can put GNU ls on a macOS box.

match.description: Conditions under which this overlay applies. Precedence is probe > platform + binary_globs > platform alone. A declared condition that is not satisfied rejects the overlay outright; a stated probe never degrades into a weaker path-based match.

mode.description: authoritative replaces the scan result's flags, positional args and subcommands entirely (for system built-ins whose surface the overlay fully enumerates). merge keeps the scan as the base, overriding matching flags and adding missing ones.

confidence.description: Trust level stamped onto every flag this overlay contributes. "verified" additionally requires a provenance block.

provenance.description: How this overlay's contents were checked against a real installation. Required at confidence "verified". Answers the three questions that decide whether a past check still holds: which build was looked at, what document was read, and when.

notes.description: Free-form authoring note. `apexe overlay scaffold` fills this with an UNREVIEWED banner; a human clears it when the file has actually been reviewed.

description.description: Replacement tool description. An empty or absent value leaves the scanned description alone.

annotations.description: Behavioral assertions that override the adapter's name-and-flag based inference. Every field is optional; an absent field leaves the inferred value alone.

end_of_options.description: This command's own parser honours `--` as an end-of-options separator. Set it and a value that legitimately begins with `-` is passed through behind `--` instead of being refused: every one of find's expression primaries starts with a dash, and `-f` exists precisely to introduce a path that would otherwise parse as one. Leave it unset and such a value is still refused, which is the right answer for a command nobody has checked — `--` in the wrong position produces an invocation that fails rather than one that is merely rejected (`find . -- -name '*.txt'` is "unknown primary or operator" on BSD and "unknown predicate `--'" on GNU). Not derivable from a scan; verify on a real installation by running `tool -- <operand>` and `tool <operand> -- <rest>` and record both outcomes in provenance.notes. Note that `--` protects the operand slot from being read as options; it does not rescue an operand whose own value begins with `-` if the command re-parses operands in a second pass, as find does.

variant.description: bsd = a BSD userland (macOS, FreeBSD). gnu = the GNU project's build, whichever package ships it: coreutils, diffutils, tar, sed and bash are separate projects, so the package is recorded in provenance.package and pinned, when it matters, in match.probe.output_contains. apple = Apple's own port, whose banner names Apple rather than BSD (macOS sort reports "2.3-Apple (197)"). busybox = a BusyBox multi-call binary. unknown = the probe was inconclusive.

platform.description: A host operating system, named exactly as Rust's std::env::consts::OS names it, lower-cased. Deliberately a free string and NOT an enum: the set of operating systems is not enumerable, and any closed list collapses OpenBSD, NetBSD, DragonFly, Solaris, illumos and AIX into a single catch-all, which is both lossy and a code change plus a release for every addition. The examples below are guidance, not a constraint; any value std::env::consts::OS can produce is valid. Comparison is case-insensitive, so "macOS" and "MACOS" both mean "macos".
Platform the reference installation ran on.

tool_version.description: Version of the reference installation, verbatim, e.g. "9.7". A verification against an older release cannot know about flags added after it, which is exactly how GNU ls --zero (coreutils 8.25) was missed.

package.description: Upstream package the reference build came from, e.g. "coreutils" or "diffutils". Where package identity lives now that the "gnu" variant covers the whole GNU family: coreutils and diffutils are separate projects on separate release lines, so tool_version alone does not say what "9.7" is a version of.

source.description: Which document the flag list and its descriptions were read from. There is deliberately no value meaning "from knowledge", and none meaning "I ran the binary" either: probing establishes that a flag exists, what the binary prints on rejection, and whether a value must be attached, but not what a flag MEANS -- which is what a description asserts and what this field attributes. A probe that contradicts the document is a reason to re-read the document, not a source of its own. Record probe findings in notes, with the command that produced them.

checked_on.description: ISO-8601 calendar date the check was performed (YYYY-MM-DD).

command.description: The exact command that produced the evidence, so an auditor can re-run it, e.g. "docker run --rm debian:stable-slim ls --help".

environment.description: Where the reference installation came from, e.g. a container image tag or an OS build.

reference.description: Citation for vendor-docs provenance, which has no re-runnable command.

notes.description: Anything a later auditor needs that the fields above cannot carry.

platform.description: Host platforms this overlay is valid on. An empty or absent list means any platform.

probe.description: A command the scanner runs against the binary. This is the only signal that distinguishes GNU coreutils installed on macOS from the system BSD binary, so it cannot be replaced by path heuristics.

binary_globs.description: Binary path patterns, supporting * and ? wildcards. An empty or absent list means any path.

version_range.description: Version constraint over the detected version, e.g. ">=9.0" or ">=8.0,<10". Comma-separated constraints are ANDed. "*" matches anything, including an undetectable version.

args.description: Arguments passed to the binary, e.g. ["--version"].

expect.description: Expected exit disposition. BSD ls fails on --version; GNU ls succeeds.

output_contains.description: Substring that must appear in the probe's combined stdout and stderr, e.g. "GNU coreutils".

long.description: Long form including leading dashes, e.g. "--all".

short.description: Short form including the leading dash, e.g. "-l".

value_name.description: Placeholder for the flag's value, e.g. "format".

conflicts_with.description: Flags that must not be given together with this one. Covers BOTH the flag the binary diagnoses as an error AND the flag it silently overrides on a last-one-wins basis. The two are one case for a caller: apexe's input is a JSON object, which carries no ordering, so for an override group WHICH flag wins is decided by the order the caller happened to write the keys in. Reporting such a pair as combinable would tell an agent it may send both, when the result is not predictable. Only overlays can state this: no help or man page format expresses mutual exclusion in a machine-readable way.

value_optional.description:
Whether the value may be omitted, as in git's `--exec-path[=]`. Such a flag has two legal spellings and they mean different things — `git --exec-path` prints the path while `git --exec-path=

` sets it — so the generated contract admits both (`"type": [T, "boolean"]`), with `true` selecting the bare form.

before_operands.description: Render this flag before the command's operands rather than after. The companion to positionalArg.before_flags, and the reason placement cannot be one boolean on the operand: `find` puts two classes of dash-token on opposite sides of the same operand. Its true options must precede the paths (`find dir -L` is "unknown primary or operator") while its primaries must follow them (`find -name '*.txt' dir` is "illegal option -- n"). Set it on the options only. Not derivable from a scan — the usage line does not say which of a tool's dash-tokens live in the trailing operand slot — so it is stated here or not at all.

long_running.description: Whether this flag can make the command run until it is killed. The claim is "may not terminate on its own", NOT "always blocks": tail -f follows a regular file indefinitely, yet the BSD man page states it returns immediately when its input is a pipe, so certainty here would be a false claim. An executor should read it as a reason to bound the timeout or refuse the invocation, never as a prediction that the process will hang. It belongs to the flag, not the command: `tail` is fine, `tail -f` is not. Reaches the emitted contract as the JSON Schema extension keyword "x-apexe-long-running" on the flag's property. Flags that merely change how long a follow lasts (GNU tail --retry, --sleep-interval, --pid, --max-unchanged-stats) are out of scope: they modify a duration rather than decide termination.

before_flags.description: Render this operand before the command's flags rather than after. The default matches the usual `tool [options] operands` grammar. Set it for a `find`-shaped grammar — `find path ... [expression]` — where the options are per-file predicates that must follow the operands: `find -name '*.txt' dir` is rejected outright ("illegal option -- n") while `find dir -name '*.txt'` works. Not derivable from a scan, because the usage line does not say which of a tool's options live in the trailing operand slot: find's predicates are documented in PRIMARIES, not in the synopsis. Stated here or not at all.
